analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal exemption letting employers pay workers with disabilities below minimum wage.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 25, 2025 by a Democrat and a Republican together and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law since 1938 lets employers with a special Labor Department certificate pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage, sometimes only a few dollars an hour. This bill would raise those workers' pay in steps to at least the federal minimum over four years, then end the certificates entirely. To cushion the change, it authorizes $50 million a year in grants to help states and employers convert to regular jobs at full pay, paired with support services in the community.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with disabilities currently paid under Section 14(c) certificates, who would see their wage floor rise each year until it reaches the federal or state minimum wage, and who would get help moving into regular jobs alongside coworkers without disabilities. Their families and communities also benefit from the bill's required services in integrated community settings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with disabilities paid subminimum wages

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, an employer holding a special certificate under Section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act may pay a worker with a disability below the federal minimum wage; the bill raises that floor to 60% of minimum in the first year, then 70%, 80%, and 90%, until it reaches the full minimum wage four years later [S2].
Four years after the bill takes effect, the legal authority for these certificates expires entirely, and no new certificates may be issued from enactment onward [S2].
The bill requires every transformed employer to pay workers with disabilities at least as much as it pays other employees doing the same work with similar training and experience [S2].

It authorizes grants — $50 million a year for fiscal 2026 through 2031 — to states (up to $10 million over five years) and to certificate-holding employers (up to $500,000) to rebuild their programs around competitive, integrated jobs and community-based services, plus a six-year technical assistance contract [S2].

States must give workers with the most significant disabilities, including intellectual and developmental disabilities, priority in receiving the supports they need during and after the transition, and people employed under certificates must make up at least a quarter of each state's advisory council [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that hold 14(c) certificates — many of them nonprofit sheltered workshops whose business model depends on certified subminimum wages — lose that authority, even with grant help to convert. Taxpayers fund the grant programs if Congress appropriates the money.

drawbacks.text: The $50 million a year is an authorization, not guaranteed money; Congress must appropriate it each year, and if grants fall short, some workers could lose their current jobs or day programming before full-wage alternatives exist [S2].

Some families and disability-service providers argue that sheltered workshops are the right setting for people with the most significant disabilities, and the bill's own requirement that states assure every 14(c) worker ends up in competitive integrated employment shows the transition is not guaranteed to succeed for everyone [S2].
Employers get a four-year wage ramp but must rebuild contracts, funding, and staffing to comply, a real conversion cost the grants may only partly offset [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers affected, the upside is concrete: a legal guarantee of at least minimum wage and eventually the same pay as coworkers doing the same job. The risks are real too — the transition depends on grant money Congress has not yet appropriated and on service systems that must expand quickly — but the bill builds in a multi-year ramp, priority support for people with the most significant disabilities, and a required independent evaluation, which makes the design more careful than a simple immediate ban.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was filed, and it has sat there since; nothing in the record shows a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia introduced the bill on July 25, 2025, for himself and Rep. Pete Sessions of Texas [S2].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce [S1][S4].
Eight House members cosponsored it: six Democrats and two Republicans [S3].
No further action — no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final outcome yet. Employers holding 14(c) certificates keep paying subminimum wages while the bill waits, and workers affected continue earning below minimum wage.

for.name: Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out Section 14(c) subminimum wage certificates and fund the transition to full-wage jobs

for.name: Rep. Pete Sessions
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction as its Republican original cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only recorded support so far is bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor joined by a Republican original cosponsor, with six Democratic and two Republican cosponsors — and no one has acted against it yet.

industries.industry: Employers holding 14(c) certificates (sheltered workshops and similar programs)
industries.note: Their business model — employing people with disabilities at certified subminimum wages — is phased out over four years and then shut down. Transformation grants of $100,000 to $500,000 per employer partially offset the cost of converting to full-wage models.

States and providers that deliver competitive integrated employment and community-based services become the funded channel for the transition, receiving state grants of up to $10 million and a six-year federal technical assistance contract. The workers' gains depend on these providers expanding their services.

industries.industry: General employers hiring in integrated settings
industries.note: The bill directs states to recruit private, nonprofit, and government employers to hire workers coming out of 14(c) programs, expanding the pool of supported job candidates at no wage cost to those employers.

analysis.trajectory: At this stage — referred to committee, no hearing, and eight cosponsors — the most common path is that the bill stays in committee and expires when this Congress ends in January 2027. It would need a committee hearing and markup, or unusually strong leadership interest, to reach a House vote; its bipartisan sponsorship gives it a foothold but not momentum yet.
